Rhythm of Crime: Visualizing the Seasonality of Crime in Philadelphia

You are likely aware of the reputation Philadelphia has for being one of the most dangerous cities in the United States. In 2024, Philadelphia fell within the top 10 cities with the highest crime rates. Despite this, crime rates are continuously dropping and have been dropping for the last 30 years. Criminologists suggest that crime rates tend to follow a seasonal pattern, higher in the summer and lower in the winter. Like other cities, Philadelphia follows this seasonal pattern, but data from 2020 to 2024 tells a more complicated story.

Using data from OpenDataPhilly, a data catalog of the Philadelphia region, I pulled annual crime reports from 2020–2024. These reports capture every single crime reported within a year and document the date, time, crime type, location, and many more variables. With this data we can look into the four most prevalent crime categories in Philadelphia and how their reports fluctuate within a year.

Assaults and Burglaries

Both assaults and burglaries follow the seasonal pattern across most years. However, each of these graphs shows a much larger count for the year 2020. When looking at the assault graph we can see that in 2020, the highest number of reports was around late August. On the other hand, the burglary reports peaked around June of 2020. You might expect these categories to peak around the same time every year, but there seems to be a reason other than weather that is influencing these trends.

2020 was the year of the pandemic, civil unrest, and the presidential election. When looking at a timeline of the pandemic in Philadelphia published by the Inquirer, COVID cases started to surge around March. It wasn’t until mid-July that gyms, restaurants, and other businesses reopened with strict restrictions, and remained restricted until late August. Tensions among citizens climbed and led to incidents of aggravated assault, suggesting that the peak of assaults wasn’t just about the summer heat.

While COVID was taking over the city, people were also continuously fighting for the city back. The killing of George Floyd led to a wave of protests and civil unrest from late May to early June. Thousands of people took to the streets of Philadelphia, and while most were peaceful, others turned to breaking into businesses in Center City. This timeline aligns with what is illustrated in the graphic above, indicating that significant events such as civil unrest can alter seasonal crime trends.

Theft

Similar to assaults, COVID seems to have had a notable impact on theft trends. The pandemic limited people from going outside, which ultimately reduced the number of targets for offenders to steal from. The data reflects this—2020 shows a significant dip, followed by a steady incline in the following years, as restrictions were lifted and daily life resumed.

Fraud

Fraud is the most interesting and unpredictable of the four categories. Unlike the other categories, it doesn’t follow a clear seasonal arc. The reports have been high in both January and July. Fraud is often conducted online, making the usual logic of “more people being outside” not applicable. The higher rates in both the winter and summer might be pointing to something else: holiday shopping and vacation scams.

Philadelphia’s crime is seasonal. However, the data shows that this season doesn’t just rely on the weather. Pandemics, protests, and presents all left a significant mark on five years of crime reports. Crime is a response to everything that happens, whether that’s environmental or social.
